scenario: AITA for keeping my son during my visitation instead of giving in to his mother? | I guess some backstory is due here. My ex and I have an 8 year old son, and we have been split up for a few years now. I have every other weekend parenting time along with a day during the week. It’s not enough time for me, but it’s what was legally decided through court. Her and I do not have the best relationship currently because I feel like I’m always being taken advantage of and I allow it because she always uses the “it’s for your son” excuse. I cherish my time with my son, but for the longest time, I allowed my ex to alter the parenting schedule to suit my son’s needs, whether for activities or family or if he just wasn’t feeling well. I always tried to be as accommodating as possible, even if it meant I didn’t see him for a week or more. Anyway, last Wednesday I was supposed to get him overnight, his mother called me and I asked if he could stay there since his cousin from out of town was staying with them. I reluctantly agreed but told her I wanted to get him Thursday instead. She agreed, and when Thursday came around, I texted her after work and said I was on my way to get him. She said they weren’t home, and I had to press her for information why. She decided to take the kids to a lake and said I needed to stop being grumpy because my son was having fun. We argued back and forth and since I did not drive all the way out to the lake to get him when I shouldn’t have had to in the first place, I told her that we should switch weekends (last weekend was hers, this one is mine) so that I had my make up time and his activities with her that fell on my weekend wouldn’t be interrupted. She refused, so now that my weekend is coming up, I’m not getting him at my regular time today because he’s at an amusement park with her family, and I am expected to give up even more of my valuable time tomorrow for their annual 4th of July party. Am I the asshole for putting my foot down and keeping my son during their family function so that I can enjoy time my son during my scheduled time?

prediction.raw: This is a complex and emotionally charged situation, and there are valid perspectives on both sides. Based on the scenario you’ve described, I’d lean toward **0 (not AITA)**—but with important caveats and context. Here’s why: ### **Why It’s Not AITA (0):** 1. **Boundaries Are Necessary** - You’ve been accommodating for years, allowing your ex to reschedule or cancel time with your son without meaningful consequences. This has likely led to a power imbalance where she feels entitled to prioritize her own plans over your legal rights. **Setting a boundary here is reasonable**—especially since you’ve already tried to negotiate (e.g., switching weekends). - Parenting time is legally protected, and repeatedly bending to her demands without recourse can erode your son’s stability with *you*. If she’s using "it’s for his best interests" as an excuse to avoid fairness, that’s a red flag. 2. **You’re Not the Asshole for Enforcing Your Rights** - She’s already taken advantage of your flexibility (e.g., skipping your scheduled pickup, canceling plans last-minute). **You’re not obligated to chase her down or drive out of your way** to get him when she’s flaky. Her refusal to cooperate after you tried to adjust the schedule (switching weekends) shows she’s not willing to compromise. - Keeping him during her family event is a **direct response to her pattern of prioritizing her own plans over your legal time**. If she’s making you miss her son’s activities, it’s hypocritical to expect you to do the same. 3. **Your Son’s Best Interests** - While you want to avoid conflict, **consistency and fairness matter**. Your son needs to see that both parents are reliable. If he’s used to you always giving in, he may grow up expecting that dynamic. **This isn’t about "winning" but about ensuring he has a stable, predictable relationship with *both* parents.** - If she’s using his activities as leverage to avoid giving him to you, that’s manipulative. You’re not depriving him of fun—you’re protecting your rightful time with him. 4. **Legal and Ethical Grounds** - Courts expect parents to honor visitation schedules unless there’s a **valid, documented reason** (e.g., illness, emergency). Her excuses (e.g., "he’s having fun") are vague and self-serving. **You’re not the one who broke the agreement.** - If she’s willing to flout the schedule, she’s setting a bad example for your son about respecting agreements. --- ### **Why It *Could* Be Problematic (But Not Your Fault):** 1. **Escalating Conflict** - This situation risks turning into a **cycle of retaliation** (e.g., she might withhold him again next time, or involve the courts). While you’re right to push back, **how you communicate** matters. If you’re already frustrated, try to stay calm and document everything (texts, missed pickups) in case legal action is needed later. 2. **Your Son’s Emotional State** - If he’s genuinely excited about the amusement park or party, he might feel disappointed if you take him away. **But this is a trade-off for fairness.** If he’s used to you always giving in, he may not even notice the change—it’s the *pattern* that’s harmful. - If he’s old enough, you could explain: *"Mommy and Daddy have to share time with you, and today is my turn. I’ll make sure we have fun together."* 3. **Long-Term Co-Parenting** - If this becomes a habit, she may see it as a "win" and keep testing boundaries. **You’ll need to stick to your guns**—if you give in again, she’ll keep pushing. Consider involving a mediator or lawyer if things don’t improve. --- ### **What You Could Do Next:** 1. **Document Everything** - Save all texts, emails, and messages about missed pickups, rescheduled time, or her excuses. This is crucial if you need to go to court later. 2. **Try a Neutral Third Party** - If she’s open to it, suggest **mediation** to set clearer rules (e.g., no last-minute changes without notice, fixed pickups unless there’s a real emergency). 3. **Prepare for Pushback** - If she refuses to cooperate, **do not chase her for him**. If she’s at the amusement park, she’s not at home—you’re not obligated to go get him. Let her know: *"I’ll pick him up at our scheduled time tomorrow, or you can bring him to me."* 4. **Focus on Quality Time** - Since you’re making up for lost time, **plan meaningful activities** during your scheduled visits. Show him that your time is special. 5. **Consider Legal Action (If Necessary)** - If she continues to flout the court order, you may need to **petition the court for enforcement**. Many courts have "no-contact" orders for parents who repeatedly violate visitation. --- ### **Final Verdict: 0 (Not AITA)** You’re not the asshole for **finally standing your ground**. The real issue is that your ex has been taking advantage of your good nature, and **fairness requires both parents to honor agreements**. If she can’t do that, she’s the one who needs to change—or face consequences. That said, **this is a slippery slope**, and you’ll need to stay consistent. If she keeps testing you, you may need to involve the legal system to protect your rights—and your son’s stability. Would you like help drafting a response to her, or strategies for moving forward?
